narrative.text: JSTOR cover page and citation metadata for John Milnor's paper "Link Groups", published in The Annals of Mathematics, Second Series, Vol. 59, No. 2 (March 1954), pp. 177–195.

Summarizes the paper's study of links under link homotopy (where distinct components remain disjoint while individual components may self-intersect) via the link group G(L)/E(L), and begins Section 2 ("The basic theorems") by defining proper n-links in an open triangulated 3-manifold M, link homotopy, the sublink kernel A_i(L) = ker(G(L) -> G(L_i)), and the normal subgroup E = [A_1][A_2]...[A_n].

Completes the definition of the link group G(L)/E(L) (giving an alternative loop-equivalence characterization), states Lemma 1 on approximating maps of 1-complexes into M by homotopic polygonal homeomorphisms, and states and begins proving Lemma 2, a Lefschetz-duality isomorphism between singular homology H_r(U - V, X) and Cech-Dowker cohomology H^{n-r}(U - X u inf, V u inf).

Completes the direct-limit proof of Lemma 2, proves Lemma 3 using mapping cylinders to show that a homotopy between homeomorphisms h_0, h_1 : Y -> Z induces an isomorphism H^r(Z, h_0(Y)) ~= H^r(Z, h_1(Y)), and begins the proof of Theorem 1 (homotopy invariance of the link group G(L)/E(L)) with Case 1 (1-links) by interpreting G/[A] via the universal cover U of M and H_1(U - V, X).

Completes the proof of Theorem 1 by showing G/[A] is homotopy invariant via Lemmas 2 and 3 (Case 1), extending invariance to homotopies moving a single component of an n-link (Case 2) and arbitrary homotopies via polygonal approximation (Case 3), and begins defining meridians in the link group for an oriented manifold M.

Defines the i-th meridian alpha_i, the kernel a_i = ker(G(L)/E(L) -> G(L_i)/E(L_i)), and the i-th parallel coset beta_i a_i, states Theorem 2 (the homotopy isomorphism preserves meridian-parallel pairs (alpha_i, beta_i a_i) up to conjugation), proves Lemma 4 (the normal subgroup generated by alpha_i is A_i in G(L) and a_i in the link group), and states Theorem 3 (conjugate elements in the link group yield homotopic (n+1)-links).

Proves Theorem 3 by deforming commutators of meridians in 3-cell neighborhoods to a point, deduces Corollary 1 (a loop f represents the identity in the link group if and only if (L, f) is (n+1)-trivial) and Corollary 2 (L is i-trivial if and only if beta_i a_i = a_i), and begins Section 3 ("An example") by stating Theorem 4 that replacing a polygonal knot in Euclidean space by parallel knots with linking numbers zero yields a trivial link.

Defines the lower central series G_r of a group G, states Lemma 5 that the (n+1)-st lower central subgroup of the link group of a proper n-link in Euclidean space is trivial, and notes the connection with K.-T. Chen's lower central series isotopy invariants G(L)/G_r(L).

Proves Lemma 5 by induction on n using the commutativity of the normal subgroups a_i, uses Lemma 5 and Alexander duality on the knot tubular neighborhood complement M - N to complete the proof of Theorem 4, gives a 4-component counterexample (Figures 3 and 4) showing that replacing each component of a trivial 2-link by two zero-linking parallels can be non-trivial, and introduces Section 4 ("Trivial links") on the equivalence of the link triviality decision problem (I) and the word problem for link groups of trivial links (II).

Proves the equivalence of problems (I) and (II) via Corollary 1, defines the integral group rings JG(L) and J(link group) and kernel ideals K_i(L) and script-K_i(L), and states and begins proving Lemma 6 that the natural map JG/(K_1^2 + ... + K_n^2) -> J(link group)/(script-K_1^2 + ... + script-K_n^2) onto R(L) is an isomorphism.

Completes the proof of Lemma 6, proves Lemma 7 that every element of a_i(L) has the form alpha_i^s for s in J(link group) depending only on s modulo (script-K_i + script-K_1^2 + ... + script-K_n^2) ~= R(L_i), and states and begins proving Theorem 5 that for an i-trivial link every element of a_i(L) is uniquely alpha_i^sigma with sigma in R(L_i) by introducing the Fox derivation D_i : JG(L) -> JG(L).

Completes the proof of Theorem 5 by showing the induced Fox derivation delta_i : R(L) -> R(L_i) satisfies delta_i lambda varepsilon = id_{R(L_i)}, and deduces Theorem 6 by induction on n: for a trivial link L, the natural homomorphism from the link group into R(L) is an injective isomorphism.

Defines canonical words phi_0 k_{j_1} phi_1 k_{j_2} ... k_{j_p} phi_p (with k_i = alpha_i - 1 and distinct indices j_1, ..., j_p) and canonical sentences in JG(L) for a trivial link, proves Theorem 7 that every element of R(L) = JG/(K_1^2 + ... + K_n^2) is represented by a unique canonical sentence (where multiplying words with a repeated index k_j yields zero), and notes the resulting solution to the word problem for the link group.

Gives a second normal-form solution to the word problem in the link group of a trivial link L_n via the unique decomposition phi alpha_1^{sigma_0} alpha_2^{sigma_1} ... alpha_n^{sigma_{n-1}} with sigma_{r-1} in R(L_{r-1}), proves Theorem 8 that a link L whose link group is isomorphic to that of a trivial link via a meridian-conjugacy-preserving isomorphism is itself trivial, and begins Section 5 ("Almost trivial links") by defining the (n-2)! integer homotopy invariants mu(i_1 ... i_{n-2}, n-1 n) via sigma = sum mu(i_1 ... i_{n-2}, n-1 n) k_{i_1} ... k_{i_{n-2}}.

Shows that the (n-2)! integers mu(i_1 ... i_{n-2}, n-1 n) form a complete set of link-homotopy invariants for almost trivial n-links in Euclidean space, illustrates the cases n=2 (linking number mu(12)), n=3 (the Borromean rings mu(1,23)=1 in Figure 5 and mu=3 in Figure 6), n=4 (Figure 4), and general n (Figure 7), describes sign changes under orientation reversals, and introduces the symmetric formulation beta_r^{(s)} = alpha_s^{sigma_{r,s}}.

Derives the transformation formulas relating the invariants sigma_{r,s} = sum mu(i_1 ... i_{n-2}, r s) k_{i_1} ... k_{i_{n-2}} for different choices of r and s, proving sigma_{s,r} = omega(sigma_{r,s}) and sigma_{t,s} = delta_t chi_r(sigma_{r,s}), gives explicit inductive rules for omega, delta_r, and chi_r on canonical words k_{i_1} ... k_{i_m}, and works out the symmetry examples for n=2 and n=3.

Works out the n=4 permutation symmetries of mu(i_1 i_2, i_3 i_4) (including the cyclic and Jacobi-type sum relations), states the general cyclic symmetry (7) and shuffle/intermeshing relation (8) for mu for arbitrary n, remarks on non-homotopy-invariant self-linking numbers obtained by replacing components with zero-linking parallels, and begins Section 6 ("Arbitrary links in euclidean space") with the presentation <alpha_1, ..., alpha_n | alpha_i w_i alpha_i^{-1} w_i^{-1} = 1, E = 1> of the link group.

Proves the presentation <alpha_1, ..., alpha_n | alpha_i w_i alpha_i^{-1} w_i^{-1} = 1, E = 1> of the link group from the Wirtinger presentation of G(L) by eliminating extra generators modulo E, applies it to 2-links, and derives a complete homotopy classification of 3-links in Euclidean space via the three pairwise linking numbers mu(12), mu(13), mu(23) and the residue class of mu(123) modulo Delta = gcd(mu(13), mu(23), mu(12)).

Illustrates the 3-link classification (showing Delta distinct links for fixed pairwise linking numbers, exemplified by (0,2,4) in Figures 8 and 9), and outlines an inductive construction of general n-links yielding residue-class homotopy invariants mu(h_1 ... h_{n-2}, n-1 n) mod Delta (where Delta is the gcd of lower-order mu invariants for proper sublinks), noting these are necessary but not sufficient to classify arbitrary n-links for n >= 4.

Concludes in Section 7 ("Arbitrary manifolds") by defining the link structure of an open 3-manifold M, exhibiting two manifolds with infinite cyclic fundamental group (S^2 x S^1 and R^2 x S^1, and their punctured homotopy-equivalent counterparts) that have non-isomorphic 1-link groups, posing the open question of whether the link structure of a closed 3-manifold is determined by its homotopy type, and listing the four references (Chen, Fox, Reidemeister).
